changes.plainEnglish: No modern federal dealer age floor yet; colonial and early state rules differ.
No federal minimum age for handguns until twentieth-century commerce rules.
There is no federally licensed dealer system or instant background check in 1791.
Private transfers are not federally regulated.
Any waiting rules are local or state, not a federal baseline.
Purchase permits are a state or local policy, not federal.
Public carry rules are almost entirely state and local.
Some state felon-in-possession rules exist, but there is not yet a comprehensive federal prohibition framework.
Federal domestic-violence firearm prohibitions arrive in the late twentieth century.
Federal mental-health adjudication categories are not yet codified for firearms.
Registration is a state or local choice; no federal registry of ordinary guns.
No federal assault-weapon category exists yet.
No federal magazine-capacity limit.
NFA categories and taxes begin in 1934.
Modern frame-and-receiver rules are twentieth- and twenty-first-century agency actions.
Machine guns, short-barreled rifles and shotguns, silencers, and related items must be registered and taxed under the National Firearms Act.
Licensed dealers may not sell long guns to buyers under 18.
Licensed dealers may not sell handguns to buyers under 21.
Dealers must follow federal Form 4473 and prohibited-person rules, but the instant NICS system does not exist until 1998.
Federal law broadly prohibits firearm possession by people convicted of crimes punishable by more than one year, with limited exceptions.
Certain mental-health adjudications and involuntary commitments trigger federal prohibited-person status.
The Brady Act requires licensed dealers to run background checks (with an interim waiting period until NICS is online).
A federal interim waiting period applies until NICS replaces it for most dealer sales in 1998.
A ten-year federal ban restricts manufacturing certain semi-automatic rifles with listed features; state bans are separate.
The federal ban limits manufacture of new magazines over ten rounds for ten years.
Misdemeanor crimes of domestic violence and qualifying protective orders trigger federal firearm prohibitions.
The Brady interim waiting period ends for dealer sales once NICS is operational; any waiting rules afterward are mostly state law.
The federal assault-weapons ban sunsets; only state and local restrictions remain unless Congress acts again.
Federal limits on new large-capacity magazines expire with the 1994 ban.
Federal law still has no universal private-sale check, though some states require one and BSCA expands dealer coverage for certain sellers.
ATF’s frames-and-receivers rule treats many kits and unfinished parts as firearms, subject to litigation.

banners.title: After McDonald (2010)
banners.plainEnglish: Second Amendment limits now apply to state and local gun laws. State divergence on carry, registration, and sales rules becomes a central story—not a single federal yes/no.

banners.title: After Bruen (2022)
banners.plainEnglish: Courts ask whether a regulation fits a historical tradition of firearm regulation. Licensing, sensitive places, and feature bans face new litigation; federal baselines and state responses can diverge sharply.
